fulfillment_judgment.auxiliary_material: The specific GC–MS analytical parameters (e.g., column type, temperature program, ionization settings) were not disclosed in the text as the analysis was outsourced to a commercial vendor (Suzhou Meixin Bioscience Co., Ltd). The study focused on acetic acid and did not address inosine quantification. No absolute concentration values or established reference ranges for clinical application were provided in the text, only relative quantification or graphical representation of accumulation. The study design is experimental rather than a methodological guideline or consensus statement.
fulfillment_judgment.outline_action: Search for dedicated methodological papers or technical notes that detail GC-MS/LC-MS/MS parameters for SCFA and inosine quantification in biological fluids or tissues. Look for review articles or consensus guidelines that aggregate concentration data to propose reference ranges for cancer contexts.
fulfillment_judgment.remaining_gap: The gap requires specific analytical platform parameters (LC-MS/MS or GC-MS settings) which are not provided here. There is no information on inosine quantification protocols. No consensus statements or standardized reference ranges for cancer patients versus healthy controls are established by this single experimental study.
fulfillment_judgment.useful_material: This study utilized gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS) to quantify short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), specifically acetic acid, in human lung adenocarcinoma tissues (n = 21) and adjacent normal tissues. The authors reported sample processing standards including tissue dissection, washing with precooled PBS, and storage at −80 °C prior to analysis. The results indicated a significant accumulation of acetic acid in tumor tissues compared to normal tissues, supporting the feasibility of SCFA quantification in tumor samples for cancer research.
